scenes.visual: Title card 'Built Now, or Carried Along' over one GREEN rod with ORANGE parts inside. Same colour map as the first film. COLOUR MAP (both films): bacterial cell = pale GREEN rounded rod with a thin dark outline; bacterial chromosome = one BLUE loop; phage DNA = ORANGE strand; phage particle = cartoon with an ORANGE hexagon head, short grey tail and grey legs; food bar = GREEN, waste bar = BROWN. Counter box top right, white text on charcoal: 'cells: N' (film 2 adds a second box 'new phages: N'). All cells and phages are cartoons labelled 'schematic'; every number appears only as on-screen text.

scenes.tts: The first film ended with phage D N A inside a bacterium, and the cell building phage parts. So how does one phage, which never divides, become many?
scenes.caption: The first film ended with phage DNA inside a bacterium, and the cell building phage parts. So how does one phage, which never divides, become many?
scenes.visual: Brief replay of the first film's last moment: ORANGE strand entering a GREEN rod, ORANGE parts appearing. Question card: 'one phage, never divides, becomes many?'. Counter top right 'new phages: 0'.
scenes.narration: The first film ended with phage DNA inside a bacterium, and the cell building phage parts. So how does one phage, which never divides, become many?

scenes.tts: Scientists tested this. They infected bacteria with phages, then broke some cells open at different times. Each time, they looked for whole phages.
scenes.visual: A row of test tubes labelled 'early', 'middle', 'late' along a timeline arrow. A cartoon hand cracks open a cell from the first tube; its contents spill into a dish labelled 'look for whole phages'. Label 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Scientists tested this. They infected bacteria with phages, then broke some cells open at different times. Each time, they looked for whole phages.

scenes.tts: Early in the infection, the cells already hold plenty of phage material. How many whole phages will they find inside?
scenes.visual: Zoom into the 'early' cell: loose ORANGE hexagon heads, grey tails and ORANGE strands, scattered. A question mark hovers over the dish. Counter 'whole phages: ?'.
scenes.narration: Early in the infection, the cells already hold plenty of phage material. How many whole phages will they find inside?

scenes.visual: The question mark pulses over the scattered parts.

scenes.tts: None. There are phage parts, but no whole phages. So a phage is not split from a parent. It is built from parts.
scenes.visual: Counter 'whole phages: 0'. The scattered parts are sorted into labelled piles: 'heads', 'tails', 'DNA'. Banner: 'built, not divided'.
scenes.narration: None. There are phage parts, but no whole phages. So a phage is not split from a parent. It is built from parts.

scenes.tts: Later, the parts are put together into many new phages. Then the cell bursts open. The new phages escape, and the host cell dies.
scenes.visual: In the 'late' cell, heads snap onto tails and ORANGE strands pack into heads; complete phages crowd the cell. The cell wall bulges and ruptures; many phages scatter. The empty, torn cell goes grey, label 'host cell dies'. Counter 'new phages' jumps to 'many'.
scenes.narration: Later, the parts are put together into many new phages. Then the cell bursts open. The new phages escape, and the host cell dies.

scenes.tts: This path is the lytic cycle. The phage takes over now. The host builds new phages, and then the cell bursts to release them.
scenes.visual: A circular arrow diagram labelled 'lytic cycle' draws itself: 'inject DNA' to 'parts built' to 'assembled' to 'burst'. Small icons from the previous scenes sit at each step.
scenes.narration: This path is the lytic cycle. The phage takes over now. The host builds new phages, and then the cell bursts to release them.

scenes.tts: Some phages have a second path. The best known is phage lambda, which infects E coli. Its D N A does not have to take over right away.
scenes.caption: Some phages have a second path. The best known is phage lambda, which infects E. coli. Its DNA does not have to take over right away.
scenes.visual: A fresh GREEN rod with its BLUE loop; a phage labelled 'lambda' injects an ORANGE strand. A fork sign appears with two arms: 'build now (lytic)' and 'carry along (lysogenic)'. The camera follows the 'carry along' arm.
scenes.narration: Some phages have a second path. The best known is phage lambda, which infects E. coli. Its DNA does not have to take over right away.

scenes.tts: Lambda's orange D N A slips into the blue chromosome and becomes part of it. Stored viral D N A like this is called a prophage.
scenes.caption: Lambda's orange DNA slips into the blue chromosome and becomes part of it. Stored viral DNA like this is called a prophage.
scenes.visual: The ORANGE strand lines up beside the BLUE loop, which opens, takes in the ORANGE segment and closes again: a BLUE loop with one ORANGE stretch. Label 'prophage'.
scenes.narration: Lambda's orange DNA slips into the blue chromosome and becomes part of it. Stored viral DNA like this is called a prophage.

scenes.tts: The cell stays alive and keeps dividing by binary fission. Each time, it copies its chromosome, prophage and all. Both new cells get a copy.
scenes.visual: The rod copies its BLUE-and-ORANGE loop, grows and splits as in the first film; each daughter has a BLUE loop with an ORANGE stretch. Counter 'cells: 1' to 'cells: 2'.
scenes.narration: The cell stays alive and keeps dividing by binary fission. Each time, it copies its chromosome, prophage and all. Both new cells get a copy.

scenes.tts: Here is the counter from the first film. One cell, two, four, eight, sixteen, each one carrying the orange D N A.
scenes.caption: Here is the counter from the first film. One cell, two, four, eight, sixteen, each one carrying the orange DNA.
scenes.visual: Rods split in rounds and fill the screen, every loop BLUE with an ORANGE stretch. The 'cells' counter steps 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. Beside it, the second box 'new phages: 0' stays fixed.
scenes.narration: Here is the counter from the first film. One cell, two, four, eight, sixteen, each one carrying the orange DNA.

scenes.tts: Now look at the second counter. New phages: zero. The viral D N A multiplies by riding along with the host's doubling. This path is the lysogenic cycle.
scenes.caption: Now look at the second counter. New phages: zero. The viral DNA multiplies by riding along with the host's doubling. This path is the lysogenic cycle.
scenes.visual: Spotlight on the 'new phages: 0' box, then on the 'cells: 16' box. Label 'viral DNA copies: 16'. Banner 'lysogenic cycle: copied with the host'.
scenes.narration: Now look at the second counter. New phages: zero. The viral DNA multiplies by riding along with the host's doubling. This path is the lysogenic cycle.

scenes.tts: The prophage can stay for many generations. But something such as damage to the cell's D N A can switch it into the lytic cycle.
scenes.caption: The prophage can stay for many generations. But something such as damage to the cell's DNA can switch it into the lytic cycle.
scenes.visual: A jagged yellow flash labelled 'DNA damage' hits one cell in the crowd. In that cell the ORANGE stretch pops out of the BLUE loop; the fork sign flips to 'build now (lytic)'.
scenes.narration: The prophage can stay for many generations. But something such as damage to the cell's DNA can switch it into the lytic cycle.

scenes.tts: In that one cell, the host now builds new phages. The cell bursts and dies. The other cells carry on, prophage and all.
scenes.visual: The struck cell fills with ORANGE parts, assembles phages and bursts; the 'new phages' counter jumps from 0 to 'many'. The other cells, each with BLUE-and-ORANGE loops, keep splitting quietly.
scenes.narration: In that one cell, the host now builds new phages. The cell bursts and dies. The other cells carry on, prophage and all.

scenes.tts: So the two paths do not have to end the same way. The lytic path builds new phages now. The lysogenic path copies only the phage D N A, maybe for many generations. New phages come only if it switches to lytic, which may never happen.
scenes.visual: Side by side: the lytic circle on the left labelled 'builds phages now'; the dividing family of BLUE-and-ORANGE cells on the right labelled 'copies phage DNA only', with its 'new phages: 0' box. A dashed arrow labelled 'only if it switches' runs from the right half to the lytic circle.
scenes.caption: So the two paths do not have to end the same way. The lytic path builds new phages now. The lysogenic path copies only the phage DNA, maybe for many generations. New phages come only if it switches to lytic, which may never happen.
scenes.narration: So the two paths do not have to end the same way. The lytic path builds new phages now. The lysogenic path copies only the phage DNA, maybe for many generations. New phages come only if it switches to lytic, which may never happen.

scenes.tts: Here is the rule to keep. A virus never builds itself. For lambda's two paths, a host cell builds new phages only on the lytic path.
scenes.visual: The lytic circle grows to fill the frame with one ORANGE phage inside a host cell outline; the line settles beneath it.
scenes.narration: Here is the rule to keep. A virus never builds itself. For lambda's two paths, a host cell builds new phages only on the lytic path.

scenes.visual: Hex end card with one line only: 'In lambda, a host builds new phages only on the lytic path.'
